DALI tensors tutorial

Higher order DALI tensors are calculated with the function DALITensors. This function takes as input the waveform model, the source parameters, the detector network and the derivative order for DALI.

DALITensors[Appr, fp, {det1, det2, ...}, n]

Calculates the DALI tensors for the waveform model Appr, with source parameters fp and the detector network {det1, det2, ...} up to derivative order n.

Parameters

Appr: Waveform model. Supported values are "IMRPhenomD" and "IMRPhenomHM".

fp: Association containing the source parameters.

{det1, det2, ...}: List of associations representing the detectors in the network.

n: Derivative order for DALI tensors. SymDALI has support up to n=4.

Returns

The DALI tensors for the specified derivative order.

The convention for fp follows section Fiducial point and the convention for deti follows section Detector association.

Example

The following example calculates the third order DALI tensors using IMRPhenomHM at the same fiducial point and detector network of Figure 5 in 2609.38399

fp = <|
    "dec" -> -0.883787, "phi" -> 6.18412, "psi" -> 0.471846,
    "Mc" -> 190.258, "q" -> 0.935815,
    "s1z" -> 0.107562, "s2z" -> -0.0254365, "iota" -> 2.60021,
    "invdL" -> 0.0284797, "tc" -> 61093.87906420612, "phiRef" -> 5.93578
|>;

ET1 = <|
        "Position"-> DetectorVertex["ET-S"],
        "DetectorTensor"->DetectorTensor["ET-S-L"],
        "ASD"->ASD["ET-15-lfhf"]
|>;

ET2 = <|
        "Position"->DetectorVertex["ET-MR"],
        "DetectorTensor"->DetectorTensor["ET-MR-L-45"],
        "ASD"->ASD["ET-15-lfhf"]
|>;

CE = <|
        "Position"-> DetectorVertex["CE-NM"],
        "DetectorTensor"->DetectorTensor["CE-NM"],
        "ASD"->ASD["CE-40"]
|>;

(*Given the total mass of the injection after 93 Hz the waveform is 0*)
fcut = 93.;

(*We take Delta_f to be 1/Delta_t == 1/2 for this signal*)
res = Length@Range[5., 93., 1/2.] + 1;

tensors = DALITensors["IMRPhenomHM", fp, {ET1, ET2, CE}, 3, "fmin"->5, "fmax"->93, "res"->res];

We note that the structure of the output is a depth-2 list of vectors:

Table[
     tensors[[i, j]] // Length,
     {i, 1, 2},
     {j, 1, i}
 ]
 {{121}, {726, 4356}, {3146, 18876, 81796}}

Each tensor in the DALI formalism is represented as a one dimensional vector. We recognize the first element as the Fisher matrix in 11 dimensions, with 121 elements. The second element has the representation of \(\langle h_{ij} | h_k \rangle\) and \(\langle h_{ij} | h_{kl} \rangle\) with 726 elements with 4356 elements respectvely. In summary, the output of DALITensors is schematically equivalent to the following structure:

\[\begin{split}\Big\{& \\ &\quad \{ \langle h_{i} | h_j \rangle \}, \\ &\quad \{ \langle h_{ij} | h_k \rangle , \, \langle h_{ij} | h_{kl} \rangle \} , \\ &\quad \dots \\ \Big\}&,\end{split}\]

where each quantity \(\langle h_{i_1 \dots i_n} | h_{j_1 \dots j_m} \rangle\) is represented as a one dimensional vector. The relation between waveform variables and dimensions of the tensors follows that of the Fisher matrix case. As explained in Fisher tutorial this relation can be obtained by calling EmptyAssociation["Aligned"].

The function DALITensors does eliminate some redundant elements in the tensors, but not all of them. For instance, the Fisher matrix representation does contain 121 elements, even though it is symmetric and only 66 of them are independent. The same applies to the higher order tensors. As pointed out in section Taylor form, for likelihood sampling it is more efficient to use the Taylor form of the DALI expansion, which can be obtained with the function TaylorForm

taylor = TaylorForm[tensors];

Now, we observe that this quantity carries only the independent elements of all tensors:

Table[
     taylor[[i]] // Length,
     {i, 1, 3}
 ]
 {66, 286, 1001, 3003, 8008}

In fact, the output taylor defined above is a representation of the following structure:

\[\begin{split}\Big\{& \\ &\quad -\frac{1}{2} \{ \langle h_{i} | h_j \rangle \}, \\ &\quad - \left(\frac{1}{2 \, 2!^2} \langle h_{ij} | h_{kl} \rangle + \frac{1}{3! 1!} \langle h_{ijk} | h_l \rangle \right) \\ &\quad - \frac{1}{3! 2!} \langle h_{ijk} | h_{lm} \rangle \\ &\quad - \frac{1}{2 \, 3!^2} \langle h_{ijk} | h_{lmn} \rangle \\ \Big\}&\end{split}\]

where the labels were all symmetrized and only the LI components are kept. This explains why we got {66, 286, 1001, 3003, 8008} as the lengths of the elements of taylor. These are the numbers of LI components in a totally symmetric tensor of rank (2, 3, 4, 5, 6) in 11 dimensions.

After calculating the Taylor form, the recommendation is to save it in a text file:

Export["taylor.txt", Flatten[taylor], "Table"];

This file is used in the Python part of the framework to sample the likelihood, which is described in section Likelihood sampling tutorial.

Options

The options of DALITensors are already described in the Fisher tutorial in section Options. They extend naturally to the higher order case.
